newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged in - The answer lies within.
newsitem.headline: Plugged in - The answer lies within.

text.p: Everyone knew the answer was there somewhere.

A person calling himself "Sommy" was terrorizing the hard-working Tamai family in a small Canadian town by seemingly controlling the house's entire electrical system, including the television and even the telephone.

U.S. and Canadian media, dubbing him the "Cyber Prankster" and the "Cyber Punk," developed chilling stories on how Sommy played havoc with the family in Emeryville, Ontario, near the Windsor-Detroit border cities, with some kind of all-encompassing, Star Wars-like remote control system.

"The lights flashed on, but she had not flicked the switch. The TV changed channels, but she had not touched the remote. There was a voice on her phone that interrupted her conversations with burps, curses and laughter -- but there was no one in her house on the other extension," wrote Mitch Albom, a columnist for the Detroit Free Press.

"The Tamai family doesn't watch the X-Files, The Outer Limits or Psy-Factor," began a story in the Toronto Sun tabloid. "'We don't have to -- we're living a nightmare of our own,'" Debbie Tamai-Smith, 36, told the Sun.
Experts were called in -- the telephone repairman, various technological wizards and even the police -- but they all left baffled.

People speculated that the family's home was outfitted with transistors when the home was built. Others worried that somebody had access to equipment that perhaps only the CIA or James Bond should have.
Everyone felt that this modern day haunting, this ghost in the machine, this technological nightmare -- you pick the cliche -- was something that was just bound to happen.
The journalists, the technological experts, the big U.S. networks, had no idea what was going on.
There was no doubt, however, that this was the day of reckoning after decades of embracing every new technological device willy nilly and tempting the heavenly powers with our high tech arrogance.
"It's enough to make you yank out your phone, smash your TV and blow up your laptop," concluded the columnist Albom.
But, of course, it turned out to be a sad little prank.

The family's 15-year-old son, Billy, admitted to police last week that he was the one responsible. Did the boy have access to an arsenal of Sun Micro work stations or possess an uncanny ability to hack into the city's electrical systems?
Ah, no. He and his buddies cooked up a little a scheme that was amazingly simple.
He would pick up the extension and interrupt phone calls. He would flip the electrical breaker to shut off the lights.
There was a dash of ingenuity, there was cunning but there precious little technology involved.
Leave aside the son's motivation in all this and consider the reaction from all of us.
It speaks volumes about both the unfailing faith and the mounting paranoia we have regarding technology today.
As Alvin Toffler predicted years ago in his book "Future Shock," we are certainly showing difficulty coping with all the changes and innovations in our lives.
But perhaps the saga of the Tamai family also suggested that the perception of technology has surpassed what it can really do and not do in our everyday lives.

Never mind that $3,000 personal computers rarely work as advertised, never mind that great innovations like the Internet are still very imperfect systems to wrestle with, never mind that corporate computer systems routinely crash; we just knew that with the Tamai case, the all powerful hi-tech bogeyman was out there and that sooner or later he would be coming to get us, too.
But perhaps what we have really learned is that technology is a very scary thing. We fear the very thing we are building.
